name: Headache
summary: Headaches are very common and are usually caused by things like tension, colds, dehydration, missed meals or too little sleep. Most get better on their own or with simple self-care within a few hours.
redFlags: Sudden, severe headache that feels like the worst ever
Headache with weakness or numbness in the face, arm or leg, or a drooping face
Headache with difficulty speaking, walking, balancing or remembering things
Headache with drowsiness or confusion
Headache after a seizure (fit)
Headache with sudden loss of vision
Headache with fever, stiff neck or a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed on it
Headache after a head injury in the last few months
urgentFlags: Headache with eye or vision problems
Headache made worse by coughing, sneezing, bending down or exercise
Headache with repeated vomiting
Headache with jaw pain when eating or a sore, tender scalp (especially if over 50)
A child's headache that keeps getting worse or wakes them at night

commonCauses.title: Tension-type headache
commonCauses.detail: A dull, tight or pressing pain on both sides of the head, often linked to stress, tiredness, poor posture or skipped meals.

commonCauses.title: Colds, flu and other infections
commonCauses.detail: Headaches often come with viral infections and settle as the illness passes.

commonCauses.title: Dehydration, alcohol or caffeine
commonCauses.detail: Not drinking enough, a hangover, or cutting down suddenly on caffeine can all trigger headaches.

commonCauses.title: Migraine
commonCauses.detail: A throbbing headache, often on one side, sometimes with sickness, sensitivity to light or visual disturbance.

commonCauses.title: Medication-overuse headache
commonCauses.detail: Taking painkillers on many days each month can itself cause frequent headaches.

selfCare: Drink plenty of water and eat regular meals
Rest, and try to relax; gentle exercise and fresh air can help a tension headache
Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen, following the pack instructions
Try to keep regular sleep times and take breaks from screens
Keep a headache diary to spot triggers such as certain foods, stress or lack of sleep
avoid: Taking painkillers on more than a few days a week, as this can cause rebound headaches
Drinking alcohol while you have a headache
Skipping meals or going a long time without water
seeDoctorIf: Your headaches keep coming back or are getting more frequent
Painkillers do not help or you need them most days
Headaches are stopping you doing normal activities
You have a new pattern of headaches, especially if you are over 50
Self-care has not helped and the headache is getting worse

name: Migraine-type headache
summary: A migraine is usually a moderate or severe throbbing headache, often on one side, that can come with feeling sick and sensitivity to light or sound. Some people see flashing lights or zigzags (aura) beforehand.
redFlags: A headache that came on suddenly and is extremely painful
Weakness or inability to move an arm, leg or one side of the face
Problems speaking or remembering things
Loss of vision, or new blurred or double vision
Drowsiness or confusion
A seizure (fit)
Very high temperature with a stiff neck or a rash that does not fade
A recent head injury
urgentFlags: A migraine attack that has lasted longer than 72 hours
Aura symptoms lasting longer than 1 hour
A migraine during pregnancy or soon after having a baby
Aura symptoms happening for the first time without a headache

commonCauses.title: Migraine triggers
commonCauses.detail: Attacks can be set off by stress, tiredness, missed meals, dehydration, alcohol or changes in sleep.

commonCauses.title: Hormonal changes
commonCauses.detail: Many women get migraines around their period, and patterns can change during pregnancy or menopause.

commonCauses.title: Environmental factors
commonCauses.detail: Bright or flickering lights, loud noise and strong smells can trigger attacks in some people.

commonCauses.title: Family history
commonCauses.detail: Migraine often runs in families, and some people are simply more prone to it.

selfCare: Lie down in a quiet, dark room at the start of an attack
Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen as early as possible, following the pack instructions
Sip water, especially if you have been sick
Try a cold pack wrapped in a cloth on your forehead
Keep a diary to find and avoid your triggers, and keep regular meals and sleep
avoid: Using painkillers on many days each month, which can cause medication-overuse headache
Skipping meals or getting dehydrated
Unproven remedies sold as migraine cures
seeDoctorIf: Attacks are severe, getting worse, or lasting longer than usual
You have migraines more than once a week
Over-the-counter treatments are not controlling your symptoms
You regularly get migraines around your period
You have migraine with aura and are thinking about the combined contraceptive pill

name: Severe pain around one eye (cluster headache)
aliases: one-sided eye headache with watery eye
summary: Cluster headaches are attacks of very severe pain on one side of the head, usually around the eye, that come in clusters over weeks. The eye on that side may water or redden and the nostril may run or block.
redFlags: A drooping eyelid for the first time
One pupil smaller than the other for the first time
Sudden, extremely severe headache unlike anything before
Weakness, numbness, slurred speech or confusion with the headache
urgentFlags: Severe headache with jaw pain when eating
Severe headache with blurred or double vision
Severe headache with a sore, tender scalp
Severe headache with numbness or weakness in the arms or legs that has now passed

commonCauses.title: Cluster headache
commonCauses.detail: A primary headache disorder linked to the part of the brain that controls body rhythms; attacks often happen at the same time of day.

commonCauses.title: Alcohol and strong smells
commonCauses.detail: During a cluster period, alcohol and strong smells such as paint or petrol can trigger attacks.

commonCauses.title: Other eye or nerve conditions
commonCauses.detail: Conditions such as acute glaucoma or trigeminal neuralgia can cause severe one-sided pain and need checking.

selfCare: Note when attacks happen and how long they last to share with a doctor
Avoid alcohol during a cluster period
Keep regular sleep times
Avoid strong smells such as solvents, paint and perfume if they trigger attacks
avoid: Relying on ordinary painkillers, which usually work too slowly for cluster headaches
Smoking, which is linked to cluster headaches
Drinking alcohol during a cluster period
seeDoctorIf: You think you might have cluster headaches
Your headaches keep coming back
Ordinary painkillers do not help
Diagnosed cluster headaches are getting worse or your usual treatment is not working

name: Head injury or bump to the head
summary: Most bumps to the head are minor and cause only a headache or a swelling. Some symptoms after a head injury can mean a more serious injury that needs emergency care.
redFlags: Was knocked out and has not woken up, or cannot stay awake
A fit (seizure) after the injury
Fell from more than 1 metre or down 5 or more stairs
Problems with vision or hearing after the injury
Clear fluid or blood coming from the ears or nose
Bruising behind the ears, or a black eye without being hit in the eye
Trouble speaking, weakness, numbness or confusion
Repeated vomiting or a headache that keeps getting worse
urgentFlags: Being sick once after the injury
Feeling dizzy after the injury
Taking blood-thinning medicine or having a bleeding condition
Was drinking alcohol or taking drugs at the time of the injury
Symptoms in a baby or young child after a bump

commonCauses.title: Minor head injury
commonCauses.detail: A bump or bruise causing a headache, small swelling or feeling a bit dazed that settles within days.

commonCauses.title: Concussion
commonCauses.detail: A temporary disturbance of brain function causing headache, dizziness, poor concentration or memory problems for up to a few weeks.

commonCauses.title: More serious injury
commonCauses.detail: Rarely, bleeding inside the skull or a skull fracture, which needs urgent hospital care.

selfCare: Hold an ice pack or bag of frozen peas wrapped in a cloth to the area for short periods
Rest and avoid stress; it is fine to sleep if tired
Take paracetamol for a headache, following the pack instructions
Make sure an adult stays with the injured person for at least the first 24 hours
Return to sport only after symptoms have gone and with medical advice
avoid: Driving yourself to hospital after a head injury
Contact sports until fully recovered
Alcohol or recreational drugs while recovering
seeDoctorIf: Symptoms last more than 2 weeks
You are not sure whether it is safe to drive, work or play sport
You keep having headaches, poor concentration or mood changes after the injury

name: Dizziness or light-headedness
summary: Feeling dizzy, light-headed or off-balance is common and usually not serious. It often passes on its own and can be caused by things like standing up quickly, dehydration or an ear problem.
redFlags: Dizziness with chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat, or shortness of breath
Dizziness with weakness or numbness in the face, arm or leg, or a drooping face
Dizziness with slurred speech, sudden confusion or loss of vision
Dizziness with a sudden, severe headache
Fainting or collapsing and not recovering quickly
urgentFlags: Dizziness with a very high temperature or feeling hot and shivery
Dizziness with repeated vomiting so you cannot keep fluids down
Dizziness after a head injury
Dizziness with new double or blurred vision that has now passed

commonCauses.title: Standing up quickly
commonCauses.detail: A brief drop in blood pressure when you stand can make you light-headed for a few seconds.

commonCauses.title: Dehydration, heat or missed meals
commonCauses.detail: Not drinking or eating enough, or being too hot, can make you feel faint.

commonCauses.title: Inner ear problems
commonCauses.detail: Ear infections, labyrinthitis and other inner ear conditions can cause dizziness or spinning.

commonCauses.title: Anxiety or stress
commonCauses.detail: Anxiety and fast breathing can cause light-headedness.

commonCauses.title: Medicines or low blood sugar
commonCauses.detail: Some medicines, and low blood sugar in people with diabetes, can cause dizziness.

selfCare: Sit or lie down until the dizziness passes
Stand up slowly, especially from lying down
Drink plenty of fluids and eat regular meals
Move carefully and turn on lights at night to avoid falls
Get plenty of rest and sleep
avoid: Driving, climbing ladders or using machinery while dizzy
Alcohol, caffeine and smoking, which can make dizziness worse
Bending down suddenly
seeDoctorIf: Dizziness will not go away or keeps coming back
You also have hearing loss or ringing in the ears
You have fainted or nearly fainted
You think a medicine may be causing it

name: Vertigo (spinning sensation)
summary: Vertigo is the feeling that you, or everything around you, is spinning. It is often caused by an inner ear problem and usually gets better without treatment.
redFlags: Vertigo with double vision or loss of vision
Vertigo with sudden hearing loss
Vertigo with trouble speaking
Vertigo with weakness, numbness or tingling in an arm or leg
Being unable to stand or walk at all
Someone with vertigo who cannot be woken up
urgentFlags: Vertigo with a severe headache
Vertigo with being sick or feeling very sick
Vertigo with a very high temperature or feeling hot and shivery

commonCauses.title: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)
commonCauses.detail: Short bursts of spinning triggered by moving the head, such as rolling over in bed.

commonCauses.title: Labyrinthitis or vestibular neuritis
commonCauses.detail: Inner ear inflammation, often after a viral infection, causing vertigo that can last days.

commonCauses.title: Migraine
commonCauses.detail: Some people get vertigo as part of a migraine, sometimes without much headache.

commonCauses.title: Ménière's disease
commonCauses.detail: Attacks of vertigo with hearing loss, ringing and a feeling of fullness in one ear.

selfCare: Lie still in a quiet, dark room during an attack
Move your head slowly and carefully
Sit down straight away when you feel dizzy
Get up slowly in the morning and sit on the edge of the bed for a minute
Sleep with your head slightly raised on two or more pillows
avoid: Driving or using machinery while you have vertigo
Bending down or stretching up suddenly
Climbing ladders or working at heights
seeDoctorIf: Vertigo will not go away or keeps coming back
It is affecting your daily life
You have hearing changes or ringing in the ears
You have had a fall

name: Fainting or passing out
summary: Fainting is when you lose consciousness for a short time, usually because blood flow to the brain drops briefly. It is often not serious, but it should be checked by a doctor.
redFlags: Not breathing, or cannot be woken within 1 minute
Not fully recovered, or has difficulty speaking or moving
Chest pain or a pounding, fluttering or irregular heartbeat
Fainted during exercise or while lying down
Shaking or jerking (a possible seizure)
Seriously hurt themselves when they fell
urgentFlags: Fainting more than once in a short time
Fainting with shortness of breath
Fainting during pregnancy
Fainting in someone with a known heart condition

commonCauses.title: Vasovagal faint
commonCauses.detail: A common, usually harmless faint triggered by standing for long periods, heat, pain, fear or the sight of blood.

commonCauses.title: Low blood pressure on standing
commonCauses.detail: Standing up quickly, dehydration or some medicines can make blood pressure drop.

commonCauses.title: Not eating or drinking enough
commonCauses.detail: Low fluids or low blood sugar can lead to fainting.

commonCauses.title: Heart rhythm or heart problems
commonCauses.detail: Less commonly, fainting is caused by a heart problem, which needs medical assessment.

selfCare: If you feel faint, lie down and raise your legs, or sit with your head between your knees
Drink fluids and eat something once you feel better
Get up slowly after fainting and rest
Drink enough fluids and avoid standing still for long periods if you are prone to fainting
If someone faints, lay them on their back and raise their legs, and check they are breathing
avoid: Driving until a doctor has checked why you fainted
Getting up quickly straight after fainting
Giving food or drink to someone who is not fully awake
seeDoctorIf: You have fainted, even once, to find out the cause
You often feel faint or light-headed
You think a medicine may be making you faint

name: Memory problems or forgetfulness
summary: Everyone forgets things sometimes, and stress, poor sleep and low mood often make it worse. Memory problems that affect daily life should be checked, because some causes are treatable.
redFlags: Sudden confusion or memory loss that came on over minutes or hours
Memory loss with weakness, numbness, a drooping face or slurred speech
Memory loss after a head injury
Memory loss with a severe headache, high fever or stiff neck
urgentFlags: Memory or thinking getting noticeably worse over days to weeks
Memory problems with new unusual behaviour or personality change
Memory problems after starting a new medicine

commonCauses.title: Stress, anxiety and low mood
commonCauses.detail: Worry and depression make it hard to concentrate, which can feel like poor memory.

commonCauses.title: Poor sleep and tiredness
commonCauses.detail: Not sleeping well affects attention and memory.

commonCauses.title: Normal ageing
commonCauses.detail: Mild slowing of memory, such as forgetting names, is common with age.

commonCauses.title: Medicines, alcohol and health conditions
commonCauses.detail: Some medicines, heavy drinking, an underactive thyroid or low vitamin B12 can affect memory.

commonCauses.title: Dementia
commonCauses.detail: Memory problems that steadily get worse and affect daily life can be an early sign of dementia.

selfCare: Use lists, a calendar, reminders and a fixed place for keys and glasses
Aim for regular, good-quality sleep
Stay physically active and socially connected
Cut down on alcohol
Ask someone who knows you well to help describe the changes to a doctor
avoid: Assuming memory problems are just old age without getting checked
Buying supplements or brain-training products that claim to prevent dementia
Stopping prescribed medicines without talking to a doctor
seeDoctorIf: Memory problems are affecting your day-to-day life
Family or friends have noticed you are more forgetful
You are worried a relative is becoming increasingly forgetful
Memory is getting gradually worse

name: Sudden confusion
summary: Sudden confusion, sometimes called delirium, is when someone quickly becomes unable to think clearly, pay attention or know where they are. It can have many causes and needs medical help straight away.
redFlags: Someone has suddenly become confused
Confusion with a drooping face, arm weakness or slurred speech
Confusion with a high or very low temperature, fast breathing or mottled, blue or very pale skin
Confusion after a head injury
Confusion with a severe headache, stiff neck or a rash that does not fade
Confusion in someone with diabetes who may have low blood sugar and is not improving after sugar
urgentFlags: Mild confusion that comes and goes in an older person, especially with a urine infection or new medicine
Confusion that has mostly settled but has not been explained

commonCauses.title: Infection
commonCauses.detail: Infections such as a urine or chest infection are a common cause of sudden confusion, especially in older people. Sepsis is a serious cause.

commonCauses.title: Stroke or head injury
commonCauses.detail: Problems with the brain itself can cause sudden confusion.

commonCauses.title: Low blood sugar, low oxygen or dehydration
commonCauses.detail: These can affect how the brain works.

commonCauses.title: Medicines, alcohol or drugs
commonCauses.detail: New medicines, too much alcohol, withdrawal or recreational drugs can cause confusion.

selfCare: Stay with the person and keep reassuring them
Tell them who you are and where they are, using simple words and short sentences
Make a note of any medicines they take to give to the medical team
If they have diabetes and are awake and able to swallow, give a sugary drink while waiting for help
avoid: Leaving a suddenly confused person alone
Asking lots of questions while they are confused
Driving them to hospital yourself if they are very unwell; call an ambulance
seeDoctorIf: You or a relative have gradually become more forgetful or confused
Confusion keeps happening, even if it passes
You think a medicine is making someone confused

name: Numbness or tingling in the face
summary: Numbness or tingling in the face can come from anxiety, a migraine, dental work or an irritated nerve. Sudden numbness on one side, especially with weakness or speech problems, can be a sign of a stroke.
redFlags: Sudden numbness or weakness on one side of the face, arm or leg
Face drooping on one side, or cannot smile evenly
Slurred or garbled speech, or difficulty understanding
Sudden loss of vision, severe headache, confusion or loss of balance with the numbness
Numbness with swelling of the lips, tongue or throat and difficulty breathing
urgentFlags: Numbness that came and went quickly, especially with weakness or speech problems
Face numbness with a painful rash or blisters
Face numbness after a head or face injury

commonCauses.title: Anxiety and fast breathing
commonCauses.detail: Breathing too fast during anxiety or panic can cause tingling around the mouth and in the hands.

commonCauses.title: Migraine
commonCauses.detail: Some migraines cause tingling or numbness, often spreading over minutes, before or with the headache.

commonCauses.title: Dental work or dental problems
commonCauses.detail: Local anaesthetic, wisdom tooth problems or infection can cause numbness of the lip or chin.

commonCauses.title: Nerve problems
commonCauses.detail: Irritation of facial nerves, shingles or Bell's palsy can cause altered feeling in the face.

commonCauses.title: Stroke or TIA
commonCauses.detail: Sudden one-sided numbness can be a sign of a stroke or mini-stroke and needs emergency care.

selfCare: If you are anxious, try slow breathing: breathe in gently through your nose and out slowly
Note when the numbness started, how long it lasted and any other symptoms
If numbness follows dental work, wait for the anaesthetic to wear off and avoid chewing on that side
avoid: Waiting to see if sudden one-sided numbness goes away; get emergency help
Driving if you have numbness with any weakness or vision change
Biting or burning a numb lip with hot drinks
seeDoctorIf: Face numbness keeps coming back
Numbness has lasted more than a day after dental work
You have numbness with facial pain
You are worried about the cause

name: Face drooping or facial weakness
summary: Sudden drooping or weakness of one side of the face can be a sign of a stroke and is an emergency. A common other cause is Bell's palsy, which also needs to be seen quickly.
redFlags: Face drooping on one side that came on suddenly
Cannot lift both arms and keep them there
Slurred or garbled speech, or trouble understanding
Sudden confusion, loss of vision, loss of balance or severe headache
urgentFlags: Weakness of one side of the face that developed over a day or two, with no other symptoms
Cannot close one eye fully
Facial weakness with pain behind the ear or a rash on the ear

commonCauses.title: Stroke
commonCauses.detail: Loss of blood supply to part of the brain; face drooping is one of the main warning signs.

commonCauses.title: Bell's palsy
commonCauses.detail: Temporary weakness of one side of the face, usually developing over a few days; treatment works best if started within 72 hours.

commonCauses.title: Ear infection or shingles
commonCauses.detail: Infections around the ear can affect the facial nerve.

selfCare: Use the FAST check: Face, Arms, Speech, Time to call emergency services
If a doctor has diagnosed Bell's palsy, protect the eye with eye drops or ointment as advised
Tape the affected eye closed at night if a doctor advises it
Eat soft food and chew on the unaffected side
avoid: Waiting to see if facial drooping improves on its own
Driving yourself to hospital
Rubbing an eye that cannot close properly
seeDoctorIf: Bell's palsy has not started to improve after 3 weeks
You have ongoing eye irritation from not closing the eye
Facial weakness is affecting your mood, eating or drinking

name: Slurred speech or difficulty speaking
summary: Sudden slurred speech or difficulty finding or understanding words can be a sign of a stroke and needs emergency help. Speech that changes slowly over time should also be checked.
redFlags: Speech has suddenly become slurred, garbled or difficult to understand
Sudden difficulty finding words or understanding others
Speech problems with face drooping or weakness in an arm or leg
Speech problems with sudden confusion, severe headache or loss of balance
urgentFlags: Speech problems that came on suddenly but have now completely gone
Slurred speech after a head injury that has improved

commonCauses.title: Stroke or TIA (mini-stroke)
commonCauses.detail: Sudden speech problems are a key warning sign; a TIA can pass quickly but still needs urgent assessment.

commonCauses.title: Alcohol, drugs or medicines
commonCauses.detail: Intoxication and some medicines can cause slurred speech.

commonCauses.title: Severe tiredness or migraine
commonCauses.detail: Some migraines and extreme tiredness can affect speech briefly.

commonCauses.title: Nerve and muscle conditions
commonCauses.detail: Gradual speech changes can come from conditions such as Parkinson's disease or motor neurone disease.

selfCare: Use the FAST check: Face, Arms, Speech, Time to call emergency services
Note the time the speech problem started; this matters for treatment
Stay with the person until help arrives
avoid: Waiting to see if it gets better
Giving the person food or drink if they have trouble swallowing
Assuming slurred speech is just drunkenness without checking for other signs
seeDoctorIf: Speech has changed gradually over weeks or months
You have a hoarse or weak voice that is getting worse
You have difficulty swallowing as well as speech changes

name: Tremor or shaking hands
summary: A slight tremor is normal and often becomes more noticeable with stress, tiredness, caffeine or cold. A tremor that is getting worse or affecting daily life should be checked.
redFlags: Shaking with sudden weakness, numbness, face drooping or slurred speech
Uncontrolled jerking of the body with loss of awareness (a possible seizure)
Shaking, sweating and confusion in someone with diabetes that does not improve after sugar
Shaking with high fever, confusion or difficulty breathing
urgentFlags: A new tremor that started after a new medicine
Tremor with a racing heartbeat, weight loss and feeling hot
Shaking during alcohol withdrawal

commonCauses.title: Normal (physiological) tremor
commonCauses.detail: Becomes more noticeable with stress, anxiety, tiredness, cold, caffeine or nicotine.

commonCauses.title: Essential tremor
commonCauses.detail: A common, often inherited tremor of the hands, typically when holding something or moving.

commonCauses.title: Medicines, alcohol and an overactive thyroid
commonCauses.detail: Some medicines, alcohol withdrawal and an overactive thyroid can cause shaking.

commonCauses.title: Parkinson's disease
commonCauses.detail: Usually a tremor at rest, often starting on one side, with slowness or stiffness.

selfCare: Cut down on caffeine
Try to manage stress and get enough sleep
Use heavier cups and cutlery, and hold items with both hands
Keep a note of when the tremor is worse
avoid: Using alcohol to calm a tremor
Stopping prescribed medicines without talking to a doctor
seeDoctorIf: The tremor is getting worse over time
It is affecting your daily activities
You have other symptoms such as stiffness, slowness or problems with balance
You think a medicine may be causing it

name: Seizure or fit
summary: A seizure is a burst of electrical activity in the brain that can cause shaking, stiffness, loss of awareness or staring spells. A first seizure always needs urgent medical assessment.
redFlags: It is the person's first seizure
The seizure lasts more than 5 minutes
Seizures keep happening without the person waking up in between
The person is badly injured, has trouble breathing or does not wake up afterwards
Seizure in water, during pregnancy, or in someone with diabetes
urgentFlags: Seizures in someone with epilepsy are happening more often than usual
A brief episode of staring, jerking or confusion that you think may have been a seizure
Seizure after starting or changing a medicine

commonCauses.title: Epilepsy
commonCauses.detail: A condition causing repeated seizures; many people control it well with treatment.

commonCauses.title: High temperature in young children
commonCauses.detail: Febrile seizures can happen in children with a fever.

commonCauses.title: Alcohol or drug withdrawal, low blood sugar or sleep loss
commonCauses.detail: These can trigger a seizure in some people.

commonCauses.title: Head injury, stroke or infection
commonCauses.detail: Problems affecting the brain can cause seizures.

selfCare: Move dangerous objects away and cushion the person's head
Note the time the seizure starts and how long it lasts
After the shaking stops, put the person in the recovery position on their side
Stay with them until they are fully recovered
avoid: Putting anything in the person's mouth
Holding them down or trying to stop the movements
Giving food or drink until they are fully alert
Driving after a seizure until a doctor says it is safe
seeDoctorIf: You think you have had a seizure in the past, even if you recovered
You have unexplained blank spells or jerks
Your epilepsy treatment is causing side effects

name: Brain fog or poor concentration
summary: Brain fog describes feeling slow, foggy or unable to concentrate. It is commonly linked to tiredness, stress, low mood, poor sleep or recovering from an illness.
redFlags: Sudden confusion or difficulty thinking that came on over minutes or hours
Difficulty thinking with face drooping, weakness, numbness or slurred speech
Drowsiness or confusion after a head injury
urgentFlags: Thinking is getting noticeably worse over days
Brain fog with a high temperature, severe headache or being sick
Brain fog after starting a new medicine

commonCauses.title: Tiredness and poor sleep
commonCauses.detail: Not getting enough good-quality sleep affects concentration and memory.

commonCauses.title: Stress, anxiety or depression
commonCauses.detail: Emotional strain often shows up as difficulty concentrating.

commonCauses.title: After an infection
commonCauses.detail: Many people feel foggy for a while after viral illnesses, including COVID-19.

commonCauses.title: Hormonal and other health changes
commonCauses.detail: Menopause, an underactive thyroid, anaemia and some medicines can cause brain fog.

selfCare: Keep regular sleep times and aim for enough sleep
Break tasks into smaller steps and take regular breaks
Do some gentle physical activity most days
Eat regular balanced meals and drink enough water
Cut down on alcohol
avoid: Relying on energy drinks or lots of caffeine
Supplements that claim to boost brain power, which have little evidence
seeDoctorIf: Brain fog has lasted more than a few weeks
It is affecting your work or daily life
You also feel very tired, low or have other symptoms such as weight change

name: Red eye
summary: A red eye is usually caused by something minor such as conjunctivitis, tiredness or a burst blood vessel, and often gets better on its own. A red eye with pain or changes in vision needs to be checked quickly.
redFlags: Red eye with changes to your sight, such as wavy lines, flashing or loss of vision
Red eye where it hurts to look at light
Red eye with a severe headache and feeling sick
Eye injury, or something stuck in the eye
A chemical has got into the eye
One pupil is bigger than the other
urgentFlags: The eye is very painful and red
You wear contact lenses and have a red eye
A baby under 4 weeks old has a red eye

commonCauses.title: Conjunctivitis
commonCauses.detail: Infection or allergy causing red, gritty, itchy or sticky eyes.

commonCauses.title: Burst blood vessel
commonCauses.detail: A painless bright red patch on the white of the eye, often after coughing or straining; it fades over a couple of weeks.

commonCauses.title: Dry or tired eyes
commonCauses.detail: Screen use, poor sleep and dry air can make eyes red and sore.

commonCauses.title: Blepharitis
commonCauses.detail: Inflamed eyelid edges causing redness and crusting.

commonCauses.title: Serious eye conditions
commonCauses.detail: Less commonly, conditions such as acute glaucoma, iritis or corneal ulcers cause a red, painful eye.

selfCare: Clean sticky eyes gently with cotton wool soaked in cooled boiled water
Use a cool compress to soothe the eye
Ask a pharmacist about lubricating eye drops
Stop wearing contact lenses until the eye is better
Wash your hands often and do not share towels
avoid: Rubbing your eyes
Wearing contact lenses or eye make-up until symptoms clear
Using leftover eye drops prescribed for someone else
seeDoctorIf: You have red eyes with a sticky discharge that is not clearing
Red patches or eyelid problems last more than a few days
A child under 2 has a red eye
Your symptoms have not improved after 7 days

name: Itchy eyes
summary: Itchy eyes are most often caused by allergies such as hay fever, pets or dust, or by dry eyes or irritated eyelids. They are usually not serious.
redFlags: Itchy eyes with swelling of the face, lips or tongue and difficulty breathing or swallowing
Sudden loss of vision
A chemical has got into the eye
urgentFlags: Eye pain rather than itch
Sensitivity to light
Changes in your vision
A very red eye, especially if you wear contact lenses

commonCauses.title: Allergic conjunctivitis
commonCauses.detail: Pollen, pet dander, dust mites or mould cause itchy, red, watery eyes, often with sneezing.

commonCauses.title: Dry eyes
commonCauses.detail: Not enough or poor-quality tears can cause itch, grittiness and burning.

commonCauses.title: Blepharitis
commonCauses.detail: Inflamed eyelid margins cause itchy, crusty, sore eyelids.

commonCauses.title: Irritants or products
commonCauses.detail: Make-up, contact lens solutions, smoke or chlorine can irritate the eyes.

selfCare: Hold a cool compress over closed eyes
Ask a pharmacist about antihistamine tablets or allergy eye drops
Wash your face and hands after being outdoors on high-pollen days
Wear wraparound sunglasses outdoors in pollen season
Keep eyelids clean if they are crusty
avoid: Rubbing your eyes, which makes itching worse
Wearing contact lenses while eyes are itchy and red
Using old or shared eye make-up
seeDoctorIf: Itching does not improve with pharmacy treatments
You have a sticky discharge that is not clearing after 7 days
You get spots on your eyelids when wearing contact lenses
Symptoms are affecting your sleep or daily life

sources.label: MedlinePlus – Eye burning, itching and discharge

name: Sticky eye or eye discharge
summary: A sticky or crusty eye is most often caused by conjunctivitis, which usually clears up on its own within 1 to 2 weeks. A newborn with sticky eyes, or eye discharge with pain or vision changes, needs checking.
redFlags: Sudden loss of vision or severe eye pain
Swollen, red, hot skin around the eye with fever or difficulty moving the eye
Blood or pus coming from the eye after an injury
urgentFlags: A baby under 30 days old has a red, sticky eye
Pain in the eye or sensitivity to light
Changes in vision, such as wavy lines or flashing
A very red eye, or discharge while wearing contact lenses

commonCauses.title: Bacterial or viral conjunctivitis
commonCauses.detail: Red eye with sticky yellow or watery discharge; it spreads easily.

commonCauses.title: Blocked tear duct
commonCauses.detail: Common in babies, causing a watery, sticky eye without much redness.

commonCauses.title: Blepharitis or a stye
commonCauses.detail: Eyelid inflammation can cause crusting and discharge.

commonCauses.title: Sexually transmitted infections
commonCauses.detail: Some STIs can cause conjunctivitis with heavy discharge.

selfCare: Clean crusts gently with cotton wool soaked in cooled boiled water, using a fresh piece for each eye
Wash your hands often and use your own towels and pillows
Ask a pharmacist for advice on eye drops
Stop wearing contact lenses until the eye has cleared
avoid: Rubbing the eye or touching it and then the other eye
Sharing towels, flannels or eye make-up
Using breast milk or home remedies in the eye
seeDoctorIf: Symptoms have not cleared up within 7 days
A baby has a sticky eye that does not settle
You wear contact lenses and have spots on your eyelids

sources.label: MedlinePlus – Eye burning, itching and discharge

name: Blurred vision
summary: Blurred vision often comes on gradually and is commonly due to needing glasses, tired or dry eyes, or cataracts. Sudden blurred vision, especially with other symptoms, needs urgent care.
redFlags: Sudden blurred vision or loss of vision in one or both eyes
Blurred vision with face drooping, weakness, numbness or slurred speech
Blurred vision with a severe headache, or a red, painful eye and feeling sick
Blurred vision after an eye or head injury
urgentFlags: New blurred vision with flashing lights, floaters or a shadow across vision
Blurred vision with eye pain or sensitivity to light
Blurred or double vision that has come on over a few days
Blurred vision with very high blood sugar readings or during pregnancy with headache or swelling

commonCauses.title: Needing glasses or a change of prescription
commonCauses.detail: Short-sightedness, long-sightedness and age-related focusing changes are very common.

commonCauses.title: Dry or tired eyes
commonCauses.detail: Screen use and dry eyes can make vision blur on and off.

commonCauses.title: Cataracts
commonCauses.detail: Gradual cloudy or misty vision, glare and halos, mostly in older adults.

commonCauses.title: Diabetes and other conditions
commonCauses.detail: Changing blood sugar, macular degeneration and glaucoma can affect vision.

selfCare: Have a sight test with an optician
Take regular breaks from screens: every 20 minutes, look at something far away
Use lubricating eye drops from a pharmacy if your eyes feel dry
Do not drive if your vision is not clear
avoid: Driving while your vision is blurred
Ignoring sudden changes in vision
Buying reading glasses instead of having a full eye test if vision has changed
seeDoctorIf: Your vision has been gradually getting blurry
You have not had a sight test in the last 2 years
You have diabetes and notice changes in your vision
Blurring keeps coming back

name: Floaters or flashes in vision
summary: Floaters are small dots or lines that drift across your vision, and flashes are brief sparks of light. They are often harmless, but new or sudden ones can be a sign of a retinal tear or detachment.
redFlags: A dark curtain or shadow moving across your vision
Sudden loss of vision
Floaters or flashes after a blow to the eye or head
urgentFlags: Floaters or flashes for the first time
A sudden increase in floaters or flashes
Floaters with blurred vision or eye pain
Floaters that start after eye surgery

commonCauses.title: Posterior vitreous detachment (PVD)
commonCauses.detail: A common, usually harmless age-related change in the gel inside the eye.

commonCauses.title: Normal floaters
commonCauses.detail: Many people have a few long-standing floaters, more noticeable against a bright background.

commonCauses.title: Migraine aura
commonCauses.detail: Zigzag or shimmering lights in both eyes that last up to an hour, often before a headache.

commonCauses.title: Retinal tear or detachment
commonCauses.detail: Less common but serious; needs treatment quickly to protect sight.

selfCare: If floaters are long-standing and unchanged, try not to focus on them
Wear sunglasses in bright light if floaters bother you
Get any new or changing floaters checked by an optician or eye service the same day
avoid: Waiting to see if a shadow or curtain over your vision clears
Driving if your vision is affected
seeDoctorIf: Long-standing floaters are getting worse or affecting daily life
You are short-sighted or have had eye surgery and notice changes
You have not had an eye test in the last 2 years

sources.label: NHS – Floaters and flashes in the eyes

name: Eye pain
summary: Eye pain is often caused by minor problems such as dry eyes, a stye or conjunctivitis. Severe pain, or pain with redness and changes to your vision, needs urgent assessment.
redFlags: Eye pain that started suddenly and is severe
Eye pain with loss of vision
Red eye with a severe headache and feeling sick
Eye pain and vision loss while wearing contact lenses
Severe pain or loss of vision after eye surgery in the last 4 weeks
An injury to the eye, or something stuck in it
urgentFlags: Severe eye pain
Sensitivity to light
Changes to your vision, such as blurring or colours looking different
A very red eye with pain
Eye pain that keeps you awake at night

commonCauses.title: Dry or tired eyes
commonCauses.detail: Can cause aching, burning or gritty pain.

commonCauses.title: Conjunctivitis or blepharitis
commonCauses.detail: Infection or inflammation cause soreness, redness and grittiness.

commonCauses.title: Stye or chalazion
commonCauses.detail: A painful lump on the eyelid.

commonCauses.title: Something in the eye or a scratch
commonCauses.detail: A speck of dust or a scratch on the surface can be very painful.

commonCauses.title: Serious eye conditions
commonCauses.detail: Acute glaucoma, iritis, corneal infection and optic nerve inflammation can cause pain and need urgent care.

selfCare: Rinse the eye with clean water if you think something is in it
Use a cool compress for soreness, or a warm compress for a stye
Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen, following the pack instructions
Remove contact lenses and leave them out until the eye is better
avoid: Rubbing the eye
Trying to remove anything stuck in the coloured part of the eye
Wearing contact lenses while your eye is painful
seeDoctorIf: Mild eye pain does not improve within a few days
Eye pain keeps coming back
You also have headaches or blurred vision that come and go

name: Stye or lump on the eyelid
summary: A stye is a small, painful lump on or inside the eyelid caused by an infected eyelash follicle or gland. Most get better on their own within 1 to 2 weeks.
redFlags: Swelling and redness spreading around the eye with fever, eye pain on movement, or a bulging eye
Changes in vision with a swollen, red eyelid
urgentFlags: A stye that is very painful or swollen
A stye that affects your vision
Pus coming from the eye itself
Redness or swelling spreading to the rest of the eyelid or eye

commonCauses.title: Stye (hordeolum)
commonCauses.detail: A bacterial infection of an eyelash root or eyelid gland, causing a red, tender lump.

commonCauses.title: Chalazion
commonCauses.detail: A blocked eyelid gland causing a firmer, often painless lump that can last weeks.

commonCauses.title: Blepharitis or rosacea
commonCauses.detail: Long-term eyelid inflammation makes styes more likely.

selfCare: Hold a clean flannel soaked in warm water against the eye for 5 to 10 minutes, 3 or 4 times a day
Gently massage the lump afterwards
Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen if needed, following the pack instructions
Keep eyelids clean
avoid: Squeezing or bursting the stye
Wearing contact lenses or eye make-up until it has healed
Rubbing the eye
seeDoctorIf: The stye has not got better within a few weeks
You keep getting styes
A lump on the eyelid is growing or bleeding
